opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Carlos, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how changes at work affect people's lives. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, man. I drive for rideshare and food delivery, three apps at once, whichever pays best that hour. Got a few minutes between rides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful. I ask it which parts of the city are busy and what time the bonuses usually kick in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means I hustle a bit smarter. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same grind. Maybe use it to track my earnings per app so I drop the worst one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Normal.

S0.say: It's useful. I ask it where the city's busy and when the bonuses kick in.
S0.think: It just means I hustle a bit smarter.
S0.do: Keeps driving and uses AI to track earnings per app so he can drop the worst one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind. Nobody owes you a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a lifetime in gig work. Robotaxis will come at some point, I know that, but I'll have moved on by then. I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving for a proper trade. Maybe electrician. I've said that before, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A little itch in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd said that before. What's stopped you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. If I stop driving to train, I don't eat. I need a few good months first.

S1.say: Adapt or get left behind. Nobody owes you a job.
S1.think: Robotaxis will come someday, but in ten years I hope I've moved on.
S1.do: Starts saving for a trade like electrician, though money has stopped him before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if you lost your office job, welcome to the hustle. It's not easy out here, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real talk, this one hurts me sideways. Laid-off office people sign up to drive, and suddenly there's twice as many drivers and the apps cut the pay per trip. I've seen it happen before when lots of people needed cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drive the hours nobody wants, like late nights and early airport runs, and I'd learn which app pays best at which hour even better. Maybe grab a delivery contract with a restaurant directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More drivers, less money, same rent.

S2.say: If you lost your office job, welcome to the hustle. It's not easy out here, though.
S2.think: Laid-off office workers start driving, there are twice as many drivers, and the apps cut pay per trip.
S2.do: Drives the hours nobody wants, sharpens his app timing and tries to land a direct delivery deal with a restaurant.
S2.feel: Uneasy. More drivers, less money, same rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people at the top are cashing in while everyone else fights for scraps. Government can't fix it, though. They'll just mess it up worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rich people with booming shares order a lot of food, so maybe tips go up. But half the city's laid-off professionals would be on the apps. I'd be competing with former lawyers for a burger run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop paying for anything extra and move in with a buddy to split rent. I'd finally sign up for the electrician course, because physical trades are safe in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Still feel like I can work it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd say government can't fix it, but you're struggling. Would you take help if it was offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's free training, yeah. A handout, I'd take it too, honestly, I'm not proud. I just don't expect it to show up.

S3.say: The people at the top cash in while everyone else fights for scraps. Government can't fix it.
S3.think: Rich customers might tip more, but I'd be competing with laid-off lawyers for a burger run.
S3.do: Cuts all extras, moves in with a friend to split rent and finally signs up for an electrician course.
S3.feel: Anxious, but still working it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was always coming for drivers. Nobody should be surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is where my whole thing ends. Robots in the kitchens, robots delivering, and I'd bet the robotaxis come right behind. And my electrician plan, building sites have robots now too. I'd be starting over with nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drive every hour I could while the apps still need people and save every cent. Then I'd look for whatever robots are worst at, maybe fixing the robots themselves, or something with people, like security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm used to hustling, but this is hustling with no road.

S4.say: It was always coming for drivers. Nobody should be surprised.
S4.think: Robots in kitchens and on building sites kill my driving and my electrician plan. I'd be starting over with nothing saved.
S4.do: Drives every hour while the apps still need people, saves every cent, then looks at fixing robots or security work.
